basis: Each quarter is shown as the company reported it at the time. The quarter to September 2001 excludes two businesses the company had moved to discontinued operations, so its revenue is on a narrower basis.

From the quarter to December 2000 the company reported “Recurring Adjusted EBITDA”, which leaves out items it called non-recurring. The two quarters you read show its earlier measure, “Adjusted EBITDA”.
The December 2000 cash revenue and Recurring Adjusted EBITDA come from the company’s results announcement as reported in the trade press; they agree with the totals in its annual report.
A dash means the figure was not reported on the same basis that quarter. The company later restated all of 2000 and the first three quarters of 2001.

outcome.text: Filed for Chapter 11 on 28 January 2002, listing about $22.4bn of assets and $12.4bn of debt. Common and preferred shareholders were wiped out.

The SEC later found that the company described reciprocal capacity purchases and sales in its reports without saying how much of its cash revenue and Adjusted EBITDA depended on them; the company and executives consented to a cease-and-desist order.

The SEC order states that in the quarter to March 2001, reciprocal deals made up 23% of cash revenue and 85% of Recurring Adjusted EBITDA. In the quarter to June 2001, without them, the reported $472m would have been about minus $43m.
A board special committee later reviewed 16 of 36 concurrent purchase-and-sale deals made between October 2000 and September 2001.
The company restated 2000 and the first three quarters of 2001.

disagreement: Pick a pair that cited the same line with opposite calls. The strongest pairs for this case sit in the results summary or the Adjusted EBITDA build: cash revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, or cash received but not yet earned.
Opening question one: you both pointed at the same line. What does it tell you that it doesn't tell your partner?
Opening question two: what would the next quarter's figure on this line have to be for you to switch?

minorityCase.infra: The case for infrastructure: like-for-like growth is positive and speeding up (7% then 13%). Deferred revenue is cash already in hand, not a promise. The cost to finish the network is falling, and completion is expected within a year. Customer lending is described as limited. A network that is nearly finished and already carrying paying traffic is hard to call a bubble.
minorityCase.bubble: The case for a bubble: reported revenue growth is several hundred percent, but like-for-like growth is single digits to low teens. The company measure of profit is smaller than the cash it received in advance, so strip that out and there is little left. Cash nearly halved in one quarter; capital spending is larger than revenue; prices are falling; and the company is lending customers money to buy from it.

lessons.head: Company measures are chosen by the company.
lessons.text: Cash revenue and adjusted profit add back what the company decides. Read them beside the standard figures.

lessons.head: Cash paid in advance is not revenue earned.
lessons.text: It is owed back as service, and it becomes revenue only as the service is provided.

lessons.head: Growth bought is not growth earned.
lessons.text: Acquisitions make reported revenue jump. Like-for-like growth shows what the business itself is doing.

lessons.head: The same lines can mislead in both directions.
lessons.text: A company that looks worse on almost every line can survive. Ask what would have to be true for each call.
